issues.legal_issue: Demand and acceptance of illegal gratification are established when a public servant demands payment and the payment is accepted through another person acting on the public servant’s behalf.
material_facts: A public servant demanded money from the complainant to expedite approval of a revised plan.
The public servant directed the complainant to pay the money to a colleague, who accepted and kept it.
The complainant and an accompanying witness gave evidence supporting the demand and payment.
Marked currency was recovered from the colleague, and anthracene traces were found on the colleague’s pocket and the demanding public servant’s hand.
issues.conclusion: The demand by one public servant and acceptance by the other at his behest were proved; the absence of recovery from the demanding public servant did not defeat proof of the offences.
issues.legal_principle: For offences under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, the prosecution must prove demand and acceptance of illegal gratification; mere recovery of currency is insufficient without proof of voluntary acceptance with knowledge that it is a bribe. The Court relied on B. Jayaraj v. State of A.P. (2014) 13 SCC 55, which referred to C.M. Sharma v. State of A.P. (2010) 15 SCC 1 and C.M. Girish Babu v. CBI (2009) 3 SCC 779. Demand and acceptance may be established by reliable testimony and corroborating circumstances, including evidence that payment was accepted through a person acting at the demander’s behest.

rule.if: corruption_trap_case and public_servant_demanded_illegal_gratification and payment_accepted_through_another_at_public_servants_behest and (reliable_witness_testimony or corroborating_physical_evidence)

predicates.corruption_trap_case: The proceeding concerns an allegation that public servants demanded and accepted illegal gratification in a trap operation.
predicates.public_servant_demanded_illegal_gratific: A public servant demanded money from a person in connection with the performance or expedition of official work.
predicates.payment_accepted_through_another_at_publ: Another person accepted the payment after the demanding public servant directed the payer to make payment to that person.
predicates.reliable_witness_testimony: A witness gave credible evidence describing the demand or payment.
predicates.corroborating_physical_evidence: Physical evidence, such as recovery of marked currency or traces of handling, supported the evidence of the demand or payment.

issues.definition: When a corruption trap case includes a public servant’s demand and payment accepted through another at that public servant’s behest, reliable testimony or corroborating physical evidence establishes the demand and acceptance.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory presumption of acceptance of illegal gratification is rebuttable, and an accused who possesses the bribe money must provide a satisfactory explanation to rebut it.
material_facts: The marked money was recovered from one accused.
The accused did not offer an explanation to rebut the presumption arising from possession of the money.
issues.conclusion: The presumption of acceptance was not rebutted and supported the finding that the accused had accepted the bribe.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 raises a rebuttable presumption for an offence under Section 7. The accused may rebut it through cross-examination or reliable evidence, and the burden is one of preponderance of probabilities, not the prosecution’s burden beyond reasonable doubt. The Court relied on C.M. Girish Babu v. C.B.I., Cochin (2009) 3 SCC 779.

predicates.prosecution_for_accepting_illegal_gratif: The proceeding alleges that an accused accepted illegal gratification.
predicates.accused_possessed_bribe_money: The accused was found possessing money established to be the bribe money.
predicates.no_satisfactory_explanation_for_possessi: The accused did not provide a satisfactory explanation for possessing the money.

issues.definition: In a prosecution for accepting illegal gratification, possession of the bribe money without a satisfactory explanation results in a presumption of acceptance.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court is not justified in reversing a trial conviction and acquitting the accused when the trial court’s findings rest on a sound assessment of credible evidence that the appellate court has improperly discounted.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused after finding the complainant and an accompanying witness consistent and reliable.
The High Court acquitted the accused, relying in part on the absence of recovery from the public servant who demanded the money and finding demand and acceptance unproved.
The Supreme Court found that the witness evidence and corroborating physical evidence supported the trial court’s findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in setting aside the convictions; its acquittal was set aside and the trial court’s convictions were affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: When a trial court’s findings are based on appreciation of the evidence, an appellate court should give proper weight to the trial court’s assessment of witness credibility. On the evidence in this case, the trial court’s findings did not suffer from infirmity, and the High Court was not justified in reversing them.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an appellate court’s acquittal of persons previously convicted at trial.
predicates.trial_conviction_based_on_evidence_asses: The trial court reached its convictions after assessing the evidence presented at trial.
predicates.trial_court_found_witnesses_reliable: The trial court found the witnesses supporting the prosecution consistent and credible.
predicates.appellate_court_disregarded_supporting_e: The appellate court discounted evidence that supported the trial court’s findings.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal following a trial conviction based on credible witnesses and the appellate court has disregarded supporting evidence, the acquittal is set aside and the trial conviction is restored.

issues.legal_issue: A custodial sentence may be reduced to the statutory minimum when substantial time has passed since the offence.
material_facts: The trial court imposed a two-year custodial sentence for the offence under Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
About twenty-seven years had passed since the occurrence when the Supreme Court considered the sentence.
The Court reduced the custodial sentence to the statutory minimum of one year.
issues.conclusion: The custodial sentence for the offence under Section 13(1)(d) was reduced to the statutory minimum.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the substantial passage of time since the occurrence and reduced the custodial sentence to the statutory minimum prescribed for the offence under Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. No earlier case was cited for this sentencing decision.

predicates.criminal_appeal_includes_sentence_review: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which the custodial sentence is considered by the court.
predicates.substantial_time_has_passed_since_offens: A substantial period has elapsed between the offence and the court’s review of the sentence.
predicates.sentence_exceeds_statutory_minimum: The custodial sentence imposed is greater than the minimum required for the offence.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal reviews a sentence, substantial time has passed since the offence, and the sentence exceeds the required minimum, the custodial sentence is reduced to that minimum.
